flagged.title: Context: Caribbean Immigration & British Identity
flagged.reason: The video repeatedly teaches that the play is set specifically in 1984 (and urges students to analyze 'Why 1984?' for top marks), presenting a fabricated date as a key contextual choice.

mark_affecting.quote: And that brings us right to 1984, the exact year our play is set. So when you see Enid trying to raise her daughters in 1984...

flagged.title: Scenes 1–3: Enid, Viv & the Obeah Woman
flagged.reason: The video invents a letter announcing the mother's death in Scene 3 (replacing the pivotal dramatic stage image of the telephone call where Enid drops the receiver) and fabricates a letter and Easter Monday setting in Scene 1.

mark_affecting.quote: Picture this, it's Easter Monday... Enid brings the girls for a reading about a troubling letter from her sister in Jamaica... Cynthia's writing that their mother is seriously ill and needs money.
The answer drops in scene 3: another letter arrives confirming the fears they talked about back in scene 1. Enid's mother has died in Jamaica.

flagged.title: Scenes 4–7: Generational Conflict
flagged.reason: The video incorrectly claims that Mai reads Enid's palm in Scene 6 and predicts a long journey (both in voiceover and on-screen cards at 06:52 and 08:04), which contradicts the text of the play and would lose marks on questions about dramatic action and symbolism.

mark_affecting.quote: Mai reads Enid's palm and tells her she's going to make a long journey.

flagged.title: Resolution & the Ending
flagged.reason: The video repeatedly claims that Mai is dying and that her candle represents her life ending, which is factually inaccurate to the play and would penalise students in a literature exam.

mark_affecting.quote: Mai, who we know is dying, hands her notebook of Obeah knowledge straight over to Del.

mark_affecting.video_says: Mai's half-burnt candle shows her life and role are ending. / Mai's half-burnt candle tells us she isn't simply dying...
mark_affecting.lesson_says: A half-burnt white candle sits near Mai — her role coming to an end... Mai is not simply fading — she is completing a task.

flagged.title: Structure & Stagecraft
flagged.reason: The video incorrectly states both in narration and on multiple graphic slides that Scene 5 takes place in Enid's living room rather than Mai's bedsit, misrepresenting the settings of the play's scenes.

mark_affecting.quote: Table and narration state Enid's Home is 'Scenes 2-5' and Mai's Bedsit is 'Scenes 1, 6-8' / 'at the very start and the very end of the play', repeated on slide at 03:31 ('Scenes 2-5: Action moves to Enid's English living room').

flagged.title: Language, Dialect & Identity
flagged.reason: F3 is mark_affecting because teaching students that Enid speaks Standard English and experiences 'linguistic slippage' fundamentally mischaracterises Enid's dialogue and the play's dramatic irony, directly penalising exam analysis.

mark_affecting.quote: She has deliberately cultivated this respectable standard English way of speaking to try and integrate. But when Enid's emotional defenses drop... her carefully curated standard English just gives way, and her hidden Caribbean identity literally slips out in the form of patois.

mark_affecting.video_says: For Enid, adopting standard English is a conscious and honestly a very costly survival strategy... rigidly choosing respectability over her own roots.
mark_affecting.lesson_says: Enid speaks Jamaican patois all through the play, even while she preaches assimilation to her daughters... Her voice never becomes English... she is enforcing an assimilation strategy she does not follow in her own speech.

mark_affecting.video_says: Enid sits caught between Jamaica and England, constantly adjusting her voice just to survive.
mark_affecting.lesson_says: Enid's language is Jamaican throughout, even though her ambitions for her daughters are English.
